questions.q: Renwick's exec sponsor asks for "one portal" for both retail partners and end consumers. What does this lesson say that request actually means technically?
options: The two audiences must share the exact same page layout
Exactly one license tier must be used for every external user
One piece of Experience Cloud technology, but not necessarily one undifferentiated license tier or experience for both audiences
Partners and consumers must be merged into a single Account record
questions.explain: One portal can mean one platform while still using different license tiers and access scopes per audience — conflating 'one portal' with 'one license decision for everyone' is the mistake this lesson warns against.

questions.q: Why would a Partner license tier be a poor fit for Renwick's consumer audience, whose entire task list is viewing their own Case, submitting a claim, and reading Knowledge articles?
options: Partner licenses cannot access Knowledge articles at all
Partner licenses do not support external users
Consumers are legally barred from using any Experience Cloud license
It would license a narrow self-service task list at a cost tier built for deeper CRM access the consumers don't need
questions.explain: Buying partner-tier capability for an audience whose actual task list only needs customer-tier self-service access over-licenses the population at a cost the narrower Customer tier was built to avoid.

questions.q: Why don't role hierarchy and sharing rules from Lesson 1 scale well to thousands of external customer-tier portal users?
options: Those mechanisms are built for internal users' positions in a role hierarchy, which doesn't fit large external populations with no seat in that hierarchy
Role hierarchy only works for Opportunities, never for Cases
Sharing rules require a paid add-on for external users
External users cannot be assigned any sharing mechanism under any license
questions.explain: Role hierarchy and most sharing-rule designs assume a position in the internal role structure; external portal users generally don't hold one, and manually placing thousands of external users into roles doesn't scale — which is exactly the gap sharing sets are built to close.

questions.q: What is the specific mechanism a sharing set uses to grant an external user record access?
options: A manual, one-off share clicked by an internal admin for every external user
A matching criterion against the user's own account or contact, rather than hierarchy position
A fixed Public Read/Write organization-wide default
Promoting the external user into the internal role hierarchy
questions.explain: Sharing sets grant access based on a criterion matching records to the external user's own account or contact (for example, a Case whose Account matches the user's Account) — scaling to large external populations without a per-user manual grant.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as a recurring failure mode in portal license decisions?
options: Refusing to ever use the Partner license tier for any audience
Always choosing the cheapest license regardless of what tasks the audience needs to perform
Letting the license choice be driven by a feature wish list ("we might want this later") rather than the audience's actual, current task list
Assuming every external audience needs Apex-managed sharing
questions.explain: The recurring failure this lesson names is scoping a license to a wish list of hypothetical future capability instead of the audience's concrete, current task list — which drives cost up immediately for capability the design doesn't actually need yet.
